---
title: "Methods"
---

Six latent-factor methods are fit to every dataset. Each lives in one file,
`R/methods/<name>.R`, discovered automatically by `discover_method_registries()`
(`R/lib/method_registry.R`).

## The methods and their parameters

A method runs for a dataset when it appears under the config's `methods:` block (WGCNA nests
under `methods.network`). Each key is the underlying tool's own argument name. A **scalar** is
a fixed setting; a **list** is a swept grid dimension, crossed with the others in the method's
`build_grid()`. A key only takes effect if that `build_grid()` uses it; see each method file
for its keys and `defaults`.

| Method | Tool | Config keys | Stability design |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pca` | `prcomp()` | `rank` (only its maximum is used) | deterministic |
| `nmf` | `NNLM::nnmf()` | `k` (swept), `seed` (swept; applied with `set.seed()`) | across seeds |
| `cogaps` | `CoGAPS::CoGAPS()` | `params` (`nPatterns`, `seed`, `nIterations`, `distributed`), `distributed_params`, `run` | across seeds |
| `spca` | `elasticnet::spca()` | `K` (swept), `K_scan`, `para_scan`, `para_step`, `sparse`, `lambda` (one value), `max.iter`, `eps.conv`, `max_hours` | parameter grid |
| `ica` | `fastICA::fastICA()` | `n.comp` (swept), `seed` (swept), `bootstrap` (swept), `alpha` (one value) | across seeds and resamples |
| `network.wgcna` | `WGCNA::blockwiseModules()` | `power` (swept), `minModuleSize`, `mergeCutHeight`, `networkType`, `maxBlockSize` | parameter grid |

**Stability designs.** For NMF, CoGAPS and ICA the question is whether factors recur across
random seeds (and, for ICA, bootstrap resamples of subjects). PCA, sPCA and WGCNA are deterministic given
their parameters, so for them the question is how structure changes as the swept parameter
grows. Every method is also compared across ranks.

**CoGAPS's three sub-blocks** mirror its three call sites: `params` goes to `CogapsParams()`,
`distributed_params` to `setDistributedParams()`, `run` to `CoGAPS()` itself. Some argument
names exist on more than one of them, so put each under the function it belongs to. `nSets`
and `nThreads` default to the cogaps controller's `cpus_per_task`.

**Threads and identity.** Parameters that only set parallelism (NMF `n.threads`, CoGAPS
`nSets`/`nThreads`, WGCNA `nThreads`) are listed in the method's `resource_params` and left
out of a fit's identity (`fit_key`).

### PCA: one fit per dataset

PCA components are nested -- the first *k* components of a rank-20 fit are the rank-*k*
solution -- so PCA is fit once per dataset, at the largest configured rank. The fit also
records `mse_by_rank`, every truncation's reconstruction error. Choosing the first *n*
components is left to ingestion and the app.

### sPCA: choosing the sparsity

sPCA runs with `sparse = "varnum"`, under which `para` is the fraction of genes allowed a
non-zero loading in each component, converted to a count from the dataset's gene number.
Fit time grows steeply with `para` and K: for EARLI (7465 genes × 189 samples) the median
fit took 1.1 min at para 0.1 and K 2–5, but 158 min at para 0.5 and K 16–20.

**How the sparsity is chosen.** We follow Guerra-Urzola, Van Deun, Vera & Sijtsma (2021),
"A Guide for Sparse PCA: Model Comparison and Applications", *Psychometrika* 86(4):893–919
([PMC8636462](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8636462/)): fix K, then choose the
sparsity that maximizes the **Index of Sparseness**

    IS = PEV_sparse × PEV_pca × PS

- PEV_sparse: variance explained by the sparse components.
- PEV_pca: variance explained by the first K ordinary principal components (from the
  dataset's PCA fit).
- PS: the proportion of zero loadings; under `varnum`, PS = 1 − para.

The authors report that IS beat cross-validation and BIC at recovering the true sparsity,
with a single interior peak in their applications (97% sparsity for gene expression).

The search runs in two stages per dataset (`spca_build_grid()`, `spca_refine_grid()` in
`R/methods/spca.R`):

1. **Scan:** one K (`K_scan`, default 5) at `para_scan` = 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5.
2. **Refine:** the scan's IS winner p\*, then every K (2–12) at p\* − `para_step`, p\* and
   p\* + `para_step` (default 0.05), skipping pairs the scan already fit.

That's about 36 fits per dataset. `selection_spca_<dataset>` (`spca_select_fits()`) tabulates
IS for every fit and marks the best para per K; those fits are sPCA's representative fits. If
the scan's winner sits at the edge of `para_scan`, the refinement still runs, the selection
table records `at_scan_edge` and a warning suggests widening `para_scan` for that dataset.
`K_scan`, `para_scan` and `para_step` can be set per dataset in `methods: spca:`.

- **Why one sparsity per dataset.** On the earlier full grid (30 datasets, K 2–12, para
  0.02–0.5; 2,968 fits, 1,451 CPU-hours) every IS winner was at para 0.25–0.50, and para ≤ 0.2
  never won. The winner moved by at most 0.10 across K within a dataset but differed between
  datasets (GSE54514 0.25, GSE95233 0.35, ANEMONES 0.45). Replaying those fits with a scan at
  K = 5 and the winner ± 0.05 for every other K landed within 0.05 of each K's winner at ≥ 80%
  of the Ks in all 30 datasets, losing a mean 0.004% of IS (worst 0.63%), for about half the
  compute. A lower scan K was noisier and a higher one costlier without agreeing better.
- **`lambda` is not swept.** We tested λ ∈ {1e-6, 0.1, 1} under `varnum` on EARLI: across
  113 (K, para) pairs fit at both 1e-6 and 1, total PEV differed by a median of 1.5e-4 and
  at most 5.7e-4. Under `varnum`, `para` fixes the number of non-zero loadings, leaving λ
  almost nothing to change (the paper makes the same point about LARS-EN). `lambda` is one
  value, default 1e-6, and `spca_build_grid()` rejects a list.
- **Convergence.** `spca()` runs with `trace = TRUE`, which prints its iteration count every
  10 iterations; `run_spca_job()` captures it and records `iterations` (a lower bound, to
  within 10) and whether `max.iter` was reached without converging (`converged` in
  `fit_metrics`; `hit_max_iter` in the selection table, where such fits stay, flagged).
- **The 8-hour stop.** A fit still running after `max_hours` (default 8) stops itself and is
  recorded as failed (`killed_not_converged`), with the iterations it reached. On the earlier
  grid only two fits ended this way (ANEMONES para 0.05, K 10 and 11), in the low-para range
  the scan no longer covers.
- **Scores** are computed on the centered matrix, matching how `spca()` fits the model.

### ICA, ICASSO and kurtosis

ICA (`fastICA`, after a PCA prewhitening step; `run_ica_seed_sweep_job()` in `R/methods/ica.R`)
is fit across seeds and, with `bootstrap = TRUE`, on bootstrap resamples. A resample draws
**subjects** with replacement and takes all of each drawn subject's samples, so a person's
repeated samples stay together; drawing single samples would leave most people in every
replicate through their other samples and overstate stability. Subjects come from
`fit_subjects()` (`R/targets/run_method_fit.R`, the `subjects_<dataset>` target); in a
cross-sectional dataset every sample is its own subject, which is the ordinary bootstrap. A
bootstrap fit keeps its sources under the resampled sample ids (`boot_idx`, `boot_subjects`)
but has no per-sample scores.

**ICASSO** (Himberg, Hyvärinen & Esposito 2004, *NeuroImage* 22(3):1214–1222) pools every
component of every fit at one rank -- seeds and bootstrap resamples together -- clusters them
by |cosine| (average linkage, cut to the rank), and scores each cluster with
Iq = mean within-cluster similarity − mean similarity to everything outside it. Iq ≥ 0.7 is
the usual "trustworthy" threshold.

**Per-component kurtosis** (Lee & Batzoglou 2003) is the non-Gaussianity fastICA maximizes;
a clearly positive excess kurtosis is the expected signature of a real biological source.

### WGCNA: one network over all genes

For each soft-thresholding power, WGCNA correlates every pair of genes across samples and
raises the correlations to that power, suppressing weak ones. It then computes the
topological overlap (TOM) -- how many strong partners two genes share -- builds a gene tree
from 1 − TOM, and cuts it into modules of at least `minModuleSize` genes. Modules whose
eigengenes (first principal components) correlate above 1 − `mergeCutHeight` are merged.

These genes × genes matrices grow with the square of the gene count, so `blockwiseModules()`
by default caps a network at 5,000 genes and splits larger data into blocks, building
separate networks within each. Genes in different blocks are then never compared, and the
block count depends on the gene count. We set `maxBlockSize = 50000`, so each fit is one
network over all genes (about 7,500), as the WGCNA authors recommend whenever memory allows.
Its gene tree is then the one the modules were cut from, and ingestion stores it directly.
Workers request 6 GB for this.

Each fit (`run_wgcna_param_job()`, `R/methods/wgcna.R`) also stores every gene's connectivity
(total, within its module, outside it, and the difference;
`intramodularConnectivity.fromExpr()`), the scale-free fit of that connectivity at the fit's
power (`scaleFreeFitIndex()`), and the `goodSamplesGenes()` result. The TOM itself (genes ×
genes per fit) is not saved; it can be rebuilt from the dataset's matrix and the fit's
parameters.

### Error handling and timings

Every fit function runs inside `capture_fit()` (`R/lib/method_registry.R`): a failing fit
returns its error message instead of stopping its batch, and every result records its wall
time. sPCA additionally stops itself at `max_hours`.

## Representative fits

Downstream analyses (enrichment, projections, redundancy, pattern drivers) use each method's
**representative fits** (`fits.representative` in the DB):

| Method | Representative fits |
|---|---|
| PCA | its single fit |
| NMF, CoGAPS, ICA | the lowest-reconstruction-error seed at each rank (bootstrap resamples excluded) |
| sPCA | the Index-of-Sparseness-selected para at each K |
| WGCNA | every fit |

## Adding a method

Write one `R/methods/<name>.R` and add a controller named `<name>` to
`config/pipeline.yml`. The file defines three things.

**1. A fit function** that reads its matrix from the free variable `mat` (or `mat_nn`, the
non-negative shift) and, if it resamples, each column's subject from `subjects`;
`run_method_fits()` (`R/targets/run_method_fit.R`) binds both for each call. Its arguments are the columns
your `build_grid()` produces. Wrap the body in `capture_fit()` so a failure is recorded
rather than stopping the batch, and return as much of the model as is cheap to store:
ingestion can then change without refitting.

**2. `<name>_registry`**, the fitting contract (the variable name must match the file name):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `global_object` | `"mat"` or `"mat_nn"` |
| `fn` | the fit function |
| `build_grid` | `function(params)` returning one row per fit, usually `expand.grid()` over the fit function's arguments; `params` is `defaults` merged with the dataset config (`merge_named_list()`) |
| `defaults` | optional default parameters |
| `pkgs` | optional packages to load on the worker |
| `resource_defaults` | optional `function(params, resources)` for defaults from the worker's resources (`cpus_per_task`) |
| `needs_nonneg` | `TRUE` to fit on the non-negative shift |
| `network` | `TRUE` if the config nests under `methods.network` |
| `refine_grid` + `select_fits` | optional data-driven second stage (as sPCA's search) |

**3. `<name>_ingest`**, the ingestion contract (`validate_method_ingest()`):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `family` | `"seed_sweep"` or `"param_grid"` |
| `sign_ambiguous` | `TRUE` if factors are unique only up to sign (matching uses \|similarity\|; enrichment tests both ends) |
| `has_loadings` | `FALSE` for a method without a genes × factors matrix (WGCNA) |
| `resource_params` | flattened parameter names that only set parallelism |
| `extract(result, params)` | one fit's result → `fit_record_from()`: rank, seed, mse, loadings, scores, diagnostics, the raw object, scalar metrics |

**Why two contracts.** The fit targets depend on the registry and everything it calls, so
editing them refits the method -- for sPCA, about a day of compute. The ingestion contract
is referenced only by ingestion targets, so changing what's extracted never refits.

`R/methods/pca.R` is the simplest example; `cogaps.R` shows sub-blocks, `wgcna.R` a
`network` method without loadings, `spca.R` a refine stage.

## Methods considered and dropped

- **CP and Tucker tensor decompositions** (genes × subjects × timepoints) were implemented
  and removed on 2026-09-29. The planned data has only 2 timepoints per subject, too few to
  fit a time mode or choose its rank; tensor rank selection is NP-hard and CP/Tucker results
  are very sensitive to hyperparameters
  ([summary](https://rpubs.com/ivanricardo/tensorfactormodels)).
- **ICAclust** (Nascimento et al., PLoS One 2017) clusters genes by temporal shape with ICA
  over timepoints; with 2 timepoints its rotation has a single free angle, so the method is
  degenerate. Never adopted.
- **Masking cross-validation and subsample projection** stability designs were explored and
  removed; see git history to revive them.

## Repeated measures: variance partition, differential expression and sample checks

Most datasets sample each patient more than once. Before deciding how the factor analysis
should treat that, the pipeline measures, per gene, how expression variance splits into
between-person, time and the rest (variancePartition), tests change over time (dream), and
checks each dataset's samples (leukocyte composition, technical scale, recorded vs inferred
sex). It runs for every dataset with a `design:` block (see Data, "The `design:` block") and
never touches a factor fit, so it can be rebuilt on its own.

### How it runs

| Step | Target | Function (file) | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| design | `design_<dataset>` | `prepare_design()` (`R/lib/design.R`) | applies the `design:` block: filters, recodes, standardizes numeric covariates, builds the cell factor, formulas, contrasts (`build_contrasts()`, `makeContrastsDream()`) and the canonical correlations between design variables |
| expression | `expr_<dataset>` | `prepare_expression()` (`R/lib/expression.R`) | the raw values for the design's samples: arrays collapsed to one probe per gene symbol (no variance filter); RNA-seq counts, `filterByExpr()`, TMM |
| controls | `controls_<dataset>`, `control_factor_<dataset>` | `control_probe_matrix()`, `compute_control_factor()` (`R/lib/expression.R`) | arrays with `control_probes`: the control probes' raw values; with `covariate: true`, their first principal component as the `control_factor` covariate |
| weights | `norm_<dataset>` | `normalize_for_models()` (`R/targets/variance.R`) | RNA-seq: `voomWithDreamWeights()` with the dream formula; arrays pass through |
| variance partition | `vp_<dataset>` | `run_variance_partition()` | `fitVarPartModel()`, ML; per gene: fractions, absolute variances, singular-fit and collinearity flags (`vp_record()`) |
| differential expression | `dream_<dataset>`, `de_tables_<dataset>` | `run_dream()`, `dream_tables()` | `dream()` + `eBayes()`, then every contrast's and joint test's full table |
| limma comparison | `dupcor_<dataset>` | `run_duplicate_correlation()` (`R/targets/variance_qc.R`) | time courses: the same design with one genome-wide subject correlation |
| sample checks | `composition_<dataset>` | `analyze_composition()` (`R/targets/composition.R`) | composition scores, expression spread, PCs, technical reference, sex check, and the variance partition of these sample-level traits |
| summaries | `vp_explore_<dataset>`, `vp_summary_<dataset>`, `variance_explore` | `explore_variance()`, `combine_variance_explore()` (`R/targets/variance_explore.R`), `summarize_variance()` | per-gene categories and repeatability, shares over all genes, the factor-analysis genes and the top 8,000, by expression and variance rank, within-person change, time-driven genes across datasets |
| plots and tables | `vp_qc_<dataset>` | `write_variance_qc()` (`R/targets/variance_qc.R`) | the vignettes' plots and CSV tables in `results/variance/<dataset>/` |
| factors | `factor_vp_<method>_<dataset>` | `factor_variance_partition()` (`R/targets/variance_explore.R`) | every fit's factor scores through the same model (a subset: its parent's design without subject and time) |
| database | `variance_files_<dataset>`, `db_<dataset>` | `write_variance_artifacts()`, `variance_db_rows()` (`R/targets/variance_db.R`) | the `variance_partition`, `de_results` and `composition` artifacts and the repeated-measures tables (see Database) |

To rebuild only this module, run the selection in Running the workflow ("Running the
pipeline"); `R/explore/variance_by_time.R` plots the stored summaries interactively. Model
tasks run on the `vp` controller (BiocParallel `MulticoreParam`, forked workers over its CPUs)
and record their own peak memory and CPU time from the job's cgroup.

### Models

The models use each platform's own processing, not the factor-analysis matrix (which is
filtered to the top-variance genes), as the variancePartition vignettes recommend.

- **Variance partition** (ML, as the vignette recommends for fractions):
  `~ (1|subject) + (1|time) + (1|group) + (1|group:time) + (1|categorical covariates) +
  numeric covariates`. Categorical variables are random effects; numeric covariates are
  standardized (a fraction, var(Xβ), doesn't depend on scale; centring keeps a coefficient off
  the intercept, scaling keeps lme4 from refusing predictors on very different scales). The
  terms fall into categories: subject, subject-level (variables fixed within a person: sex,
  age, arm), time, group × time, technical (`vp_covariates`), covariate, residual. The
  between-subject total is subject + subject-level, as the vignette's nesting note says; the
  residual fraction is reported but not used as a metric (the vignette's FAQ).
- **dream** (REML; Kenward-Roger for ≤ 20 samples, else Satterthwaite):
  `~ 0 + cell + (1|subject)` plus any `de_covariates`, `cell` = group × time. Time courses
  test each timepoint against the first within each group with at least 3 repeatedly sampled
  subjects, plus a joint F-test per group; cross-sectional datasets test group pairs. `z.std`
  and `F.std` make statistics comparable across genes with different degrees of freedom.
- **Checks:** dream against `duplicateCorrelation()` (`dupcor_<dataset>`; the genome-wide
  consensus matches the median subject fraction), `canCorPairs()` between design variables,
  per-gene collinearity scores and singular-fit flags, and the vignettes' plots (violin and
  per-gene bars, expression of each term's top gene, correlation structure, contrast matrix,
  dream vs duplicateCorrelation p-values, voom trend).

### Sample checks

`analyze_composition()` (`composition_<dataset>`) records, per sample:

- **Leukocyte composition:** neutrophil and lymphocyte marker scores
  (`config/composition_markers.yml`) and their difference, against each sample's expression
  spread, location and leading principal components.
- **A technical reference:** the array's own control probes where the platform has them
  (ANEMONES' Agilent spike-ins, the Affymetrix hybridization controls), a background
  stand-in for Illumina series matrices (probes matching no transcript), and library size
  and TMM factor for RNA-seq. The same sample-level traits also go through the dataset's
  variance formula.
- **Sex:** inferred from chrY genes against XIST and compared with the recorded sex;
  subjects whose samples disagree are counted. This catches sample annotations that don't
  belong to their arrays.

Findings (2026-10-13): in the RNA-seq time courses PC1 is the neutrophil-lymphocyte axis
(|rho| 0.83–0.90), not library size. ANEMONES' sample-mean shift follows its spike-in
controls (rho 0.92), not composition, so its control probes' first principal component enters
its models as a covariate (`control_probes: {covariate: true}`): shifting each sample by a
control offset over-corrected, because the controls move about twice as much as genes.
GSE54514's sample annotations don't match its arrays (sex agreement 0.50; samples of one
`group_id` disagree on sex in 35 of 54 subjects), so its subject and time results aren't
interpretable. Smaller sex discordances: ANEMONES (4 subjects), GSE95233 (Patient 198),
GSE13904 and GSE273700 (1 subject each), EARLI (3 samples).

### What the variance partition says about repeated measures

From `variance_explore` (2026-10-13; the numbers are in the DB's `variance_summary`):

- **Time is a small part of the signal factorization sees.** In the top 8,000 genes, time
  plus group × time is 1–4% of variance; between-subject is 35–60%; most of the remainder is
  within-person variation. Factors fit on a full time-course dataset are therefore mostly
  person-level structure, the same structure a single timepoint contains (median
  single-timepoint repeatability 0.25–0.5).
- **The main biological axis is a stable person trait.** Leukocyte composition, which drives
  PC1 in the RNA-seq data, is 40–70% subject and about 0–7% time.
- **There is little within-person dynamics to recover.** Change between a person's samples
  shares no dominant direction (ROSE: its first principal component is 9% of the change) and
  isn't explained by composition change; removing each person's mean would leave factors fit
  mostly to noise. ROSE's high residual share comes from noisy low-expressed genes (its
  subject share rises from 0.08 to 0.34 across expression quartiles).

So the factor analysis fits the full datasets and every per-timepoint subset as they are,
and handles repeated measures in how stability is measured and read:

- **Resampling keeps a person's samples together** (ICA's bootstrap, above).
- **Within-family comparisons are not replication.** A full dataset and its timepoint
  subsets, or two subsets, share people: their agreement measures temporal reproducibility
  within a cohort. Only comparisons between cohorts test replication.
- **Every factor is described by the same model** (`factor_vp_<method>_<dataset>`,
  `factor_variance_partition()`): its sample scores go through the dataset's variance formula,
  giving each factor's share of between-person, time, group, technical and residual
  variance. A per-timepoint subset uses its parent's design restricted to its samples,
  without subject and time terms.
